Family Health

What to do if a condom breaks: immediate care and follow-up

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A broken condom can feel alarming, but there are useful steps you can take. Act promptly on the options with short deadlines, then arrange testing that matches the exposure and the tests available. Washing and waiting for symptoms cannot replace that plan.

Stop, remove the condom and note the time

If a condom breaks or slips off, stop intercourse and withdraw carefully. Remove it gently if it is easily reachable; seek help if it is stuck rather than using a sharp object or repeated force. Use a new condom if you choose to continue. Record when the exposure happened, because some preventive options have short time limits.

Consider pregnancy prevention and infection prevention as separate questions. Pregnancy is possible when sperm can reach the vagina, while oral, vaginal and anal contact can transmit different infections. The type of contact, existing contraception and what is known about the partner’s health affect the advice. A single exposure is enough to ask for help.

Washing or urinating will not undo the exposure

You can gently rinse the outside of the genitals with warm water for comfort. Urinating after sex does not wash sperm out of the vagina and does not prevent pregnancy. Squeezing, straining or trying to push fluid out is not an effective substitute for emergency contraception or infection assessment.

Do not douche the vagina or rectum or put soap, disinfectant or other chemicals inside. Vaginal douching can disturb the protective environment and increase irritation and infection problems. Cleaning cannot reliably remove an STI exposure. Spend the time contacting care rather than trying to wash the risk away.

Make room for support without delaying care

Worry, anger, embarrassment or uncertainty are understandable reactions. You do not have to settle every emotion before taking the next practical step. A pharmacist, sexual-health service or urgent-care clinician can help you work out what is needed without assuming that an infection or pregnancy has occurred.

If useful, ask someone you trust to help arrange transport or an appointment. If sex was forced, you were unable to consent, or a condom was removed without agreement, specialist sexual-assault support can provide confidential advice and time-sensitive care. Ask the service about its privacy arrangements and the choices available to you.

Act now if HIV exposure may have occurred

HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP, is a course of medicine that can reduce the chance of HIV infection after a relevant exposure. It must be started as soon as possible, ideally within hours, and no later than 72 hours. Do not wait for symptoms, a routine test appointment or a partner’s delayed result before seeking assessment.

Not every broken condom requires PEP. A clinician assesses the type of exposure, the partner’s HIV status and viral suppression if known, and other circumstances. Contact an emergency department or a service that provides PEP if prompt specialist advice is not otherwise available. After 72 hours, still seek testing and a prevention plan even though starting PEP is generally not recommended.

If PEP is prescribed, complete the plan

The usual PEP course is 28 days. Take it exactly as prescribed and ask what to do about missed doses, interactions or side effects. An initial HIV test checks your starting status but cannot rule out infection from an exposure that has just happened. When PEP is indicated, laboratory results should not unnecessarily delay the first dose.

Follow-up checks confirm that the medicine is accessible and tolerable and arrange later HIV testing. Current US CDC guidance includes early contact and testing follow-up around 4–6 and 12 weeks; the clinic should give you exact dates and test instructions. If exposure may continue, discuss a transition to pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, rather than relying on repeated emergencies.

Emergency contraception: do not wait for the morning

If pregnancy is possible and not wanted, contact a pharmacist or sexual-health clinician as soon as possible. Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation. A copper IUD is another option. Emergency contraception does not treat an established pregnancy and does not protect against STIs.

Tell the clinician when this and any other recent unprotected sex occurred, what contraception you normally use and any medicines or supplements you take. The best option can depend on timing and individual circumstances. Prescription rules, cost and access vary by country, so do not assume every product is available without a prescription.

Levonorgestrel: earlier is better

Levonorgestrel is the ingredient in products such as Plan B and other brands. Many local product instructions emphasize use within 72 hours. WHO and CDC guidance also discusses use up to 120 hours, but effectiveness falls with delay and other options may be more effective later in that window.

Take advice promptly rather than assuming that passing the three-day mark means nothing can be done. A fixed claim such as “95% effective in the first day” is not a personal prediction: effectiveness depends on the timing of ovulation and other factors. Do not delay obtaining an available suitable method while trying to calculate an exact risk.

Ulipristal and the copper IUD within five days

Ulipristal acetate, sold under names including ella, can be used within 120 hours and is generally more effective than levonorgestrel during days three to five. A pharmacist or clinician should help select it, particularly if you already use hormonal contraception. It also works by delaying ovulation and should be taken promptly.

A copper IUD placed within five days is the most effective established emergency contraceptive option, with effectiveness above 99%. A trained clinician checks suitability and inserts it. It can remain as ongoing contraception according to the device’s lifespan. In some circumstances insertion can be possible later based on ovulation timing, so ask rather than self-excluding. Do not deliberately wait until day five.

After the emergency pill: symptoms and regular contraception

Temporary nausea, headache, cramps or changes in the next bleed can occur. If you vomit soon after taking a pill, contact the pharmacist promptly; whether another dose is needed depends on the product and timing. Emergency pills do not provide continuing protection for later sex in the cycle.

After levonorgestrel, regular hormonal contraception can generally be restarted immediately. After ulipristal, restarting progestogen-containing contraception too soon can reduce its effect; CDC guidance generally advises waiting at least five days. Use condoms or avoid sex during the waiting period and until the regular method is effective. Ask for method-specific instructions rather than combining emergency pills yourself.

Symptoms mean assessment now, not at a future deadline

Seek advice for a new genital or mouth sore, unusual discharge, burning urination, bleeding after sex or between periods, or anal symptoms. A sore throat after oral contact can have many causes, including an infection. Pelvic or testicular pain also needs assessment; severe pain, fever or significant illness should not wait for a home test.

Many STIs cause no symptoms. Feeling well does not prove that transmission did not occur, and having symptoms does not identify which infection is present. Tell the clinic about the sites of contact so it can decide whether urine, genital, throat or rectal samples are appropriate.

Around two weeks: chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing

For an asymptomatic screening sample after a recent exposure, many services recommend waiting about two weeks for chlamydia and gonorrhoea tests. This is a testing window, not a requirement to postpone the first consultation. Symptoms, a diagnosed partner or a clinician’s concern may call for assessment and testing earlier, with a repeat test if necessary.

A urine or genital test does not automatically cover the throat or rectum. Ask which sites are being tested. Both infections can be treated with appropriate antibiotics, and partner management helps prevent reinfection. Follow the exact advice about avoiding sex until treatment and the required waiting period are complete for you and relevant partners.

Around three weeks: check for pregnancy

Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. They detect the pregnancy hormone hCG. If you do not know when the period is due, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Testing too early may give a negative result even when pregnancy has begun. Emergency contraception can shift the timing of bleeding.

Follow the kit instructions. If the result is negative but the period still does not arrive or you remain concerned, repeat it and seek advice. A positive result deserves a conversation about pregnancy care and your options. Severe one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or fainting with a possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment.

HIV testing does not have one three-week deadline

The HIV window depends on the test. Without antiretroviral prevention affecting detection, a laboratory antigen/antibody test on blood from a vein usually detects infection within 18–45 days; antibody tests may take 23–90 days. Earlier negative results may need repeating after the relevant window.

If you took PEP or use PrEP, follow the clinic’s testing schedule rather than applying those ranges yourself. An early flu-like illness is not a reliable way to diagnose HIV, and absence of symptoms is not reassurance. HIV treatment can control the virus very effectively; confirmatory testing and prompt linkage to care are important after a reactive result.

Herpes: a fresh sore can be tested promptly

Do not wait three weeks if blisters or ulcers appear. A clinician may take a swab from a fresh lesion before it heals. Routine herpes blood testing is not recommended for everyone without symptoms because false or unclear results can cause harm. Testing decisions should reflect symptoms and the exposure history.

When an antibody test is appropriate, it can take much longer than three weeks to detect a new infection. Ask the clinician about timing and interpretation. Antiviral treatment can reduce outbreaks and symptoms, but does not eradicate the virus. A positive result alone usually cannot establish exactly when the infection began.

Six weeks and beyond: an individualized syphilis plan

Syphilis can cause a painless sore, a rash that may affect palms or soles, or more general symptoms, and it may also go unnoticed. Do not wait for a six-week date if you have symptoms or a partner has been diagnosed. Early blood tests can be negative, and some exposed partners need treatment before a test turns positive.

A clinic may repeat testing later to cover the window period; some services use a three-month check after exposure. This differs from follow-up after confirmed syphilis treatment, when blood-test trends are assessed over time. Stage, previous treatment and individual risk affect that schedule. Syphilis is treatable, but delaying appropriate care can allow serious complications.

Three-month checks are not the same as a test of cure

After treated chlamydia or gonorrhoea, retesting at about three months commonly checks for reinfection. An earlier test of cure is a different decision and is needed in certain circumstances, such as some infections during pregnancy or particular treatment situations. Ask which type of follow-up has been booked and why.

You do not need a universal repeat panel for every infection at both three and six months regardless of your results. Similarly, a persistent syphilis antibody result does not by itself prove antibiotic resistance. Keep the clinic’s follow-up plan, tell it about any new exposure and do not interpret a sequence of results without the test type and clinical context.

Reduce the chance of another break

Use a fresh condom before genital contact, check its expiry and packet, and open it without teeth or sharp objects. Follow the size and application instructions, leaving space at the tip and unrolling it fully. Hold the base during withdrawal so it does not slip off.

Use lubricant compatible with the condom: water- or silicone-based products are appropriate for latex, while oil can damage latex. Do not wear two external condoms or combine an external and internal condom. If breakage recurs, ask about fit, lubricant and technique. A practical prevention plan is more helpful than blame.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

WHO, CDC and NHS guidance supports prompt emergency contraception after a relevant exposure. The choice and restart instructions differ between levonorgestrel, ulipristal and a copper IUD; access rules also vary locally.

CDC’s 2025 HIV PEP guidance requires urgent assessment and a 28-day course when indicated, with follow-up testing. CDC and sexual-health service guidance distinguishes infection-specific windows, lesion swabs, repeat testing and tests of cure. There is no single three-week all-clear test.

How BeMama can help

Record the exposure time, the medicines or emergency contraception used and the dates the clinic recommends. Keep the next test or follow-up appointment in one place.

When to seek help

Seek HIV PEP assessment immediately when exposure may be relevant; it must begin within 72 hours. Do not wait for a routine testing window if there is severe pain, fever, a new sore or a diagnosed partner. Possible pregnancy with severe pain or fainting needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Stop and note the time; washing does not prevent pregnancy or an STI.
  • PEP and emergency contraception have different purposes and deadlines.
  • Ask for advice now even when a later test will be needed.
  • Herpes, HIV and syphilis do not share one testing window.
  • Follow-up depends on the result, treatment and any new exposure.

Frequently asked questions

Will urinating or washing stop pregnancy?

No. Urinating does not wash sperm from the vagina. Gentle external washing is for comfort; emergency contraception is the relevant preventive option.

Should I wait until tomorrow to ask about PEP?

No. Seek assessment immediately. PEP works best when started promptly and must begin within 72 hours of a relevant exposure.

Does every broken condom require HIV medicine?

No. A clinician assesses the exposure and the partner’s HIV and viral-suppression information when available. Do not delay assessment while trying to establish every detail.

Is it too late for emergency contraception after three days?

Not necessarily. Ulipristal and a copper IUD are options within five days, and local guidance may also consider levonorgestrel. Seek advice as soon as possible.

Can I restart my usual pill immediately after ella?

Usually you need to wait at least five days after ulipristal before restarting hormonal contraception. Ask for instructions for your method and interim condom use.

When should I take a pregnancy test?

From a missed period, or at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex if timing is uncertain. Repeat and seek advice if a negative result does not fit the situation.

Should I wait two weeks if I have discharge or a sore?

No. The window for asymptomatic screening is not a reason to delay assessment of symptoms or a known exposure.

Can one HIV test at three weeks rule out infection?

Not reliably in every case. Detection depends on the test and whether PEP or PrEP was used. Follow the testing service’s schedule.

Does everyone need a herpes blood test?

No. Routine testing without symptoms is usually not recommended. Fresh blisters or sores can be swabbed promptly, while selected blood tests have different timing and limitations.

Does a positive syphilis antibody result after treatment mean resistance?

Not by itself. Some antibodies can remain positive after successful treatment. The clinician interprets the specific test, changing levels and treatment history.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
